topics.title: Forms of presentation and textual presentation

learn.hook: A news anchor reading 'Of 120 crore Indians, about 69% live in villages' uses words. A table or a pie chart could say the same thing. Which works best depends on the data.
points: Data can be presented in three forms: textual (descriptive), tabular and diagrammatic.
Textual presentation describes data in sentences within the text, e.g. 'In a strike, 28 out of 140 workers stayed away'.
It suits small amounts of data and lets the writer emphasise certain points.
Its drawback: the reader must go through the whole passage to grasp the figures, and comparison is difficult when data are many.

example.q: Which form suits this best: 'In a class of 40, 22 are girls and 18 are boys'?
steps: The data have only two figures.
A sentence conveys them clearly without a table.
A table or diagram would add little.
example.answer: Textual presentation, because the data are small.

learn.reallife: Budget speeches often use textual presentation for a few key figures ('fiscal deficit is estimated at x% of GDP'), while the detailed numbers go into annexure tables.

games.title: Best form of presentation?
items: Two figures: 18 boys and 22 girls in a class
State-wise literacy rates of 28 states for three census years
Showing at a glance how a household budget is split

games.title: Presentation facts
items: Textual presentation is best for large, complex data.
Large data are hard to follow in sentences; tables suit them.
Data can be presented in textual, tabular and diagrammatic forms.
These are the three forms of presentation.
In textual presentation the reader must read the full passage to understand the data.
That is its main drawback.
Textual presentation allows the writer to emphasise particular facts.
Sentences can highlight key points.
Diagrams are always more exact than tables.
Tables give exact figures; diagrams give a quick visual impression.

quiz.q: How many broad forms of data presentation are there?
quiz.explain: Textual, tabular and diagrammatic: three forms.
steps: Asked: the number of broad forms of presenting data.
They are: (1) textual, (2) tabular, (3) diagrammatic.
Count: 3 forms.
So the answer is 3.
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Forgets textual presentation as a form

quiz.q: Textual presentation is most suitable when:
quiz.explain: With only a few figures, sentences communicate them clearly.
steps: Asked: when textual presentation suits best.
Textual presentation describes data in sentences.
With only a few figures, sentences are clear; with many, they become confusing.
So it suits data that are small in quantity.
Answer: Data are small in quantity
quiz.mistake: Thinks text is always the simplest choice

quiz.q: A major drawback of textual presentation is that:
options: The reader must read the whole text to understand the data
quiz.explain: Figures are buried in sentences, making quick comprehension and comparison hard.
steps: Asked: a major drawback of textual presentation.
In text, figures are buried inside sentences.
The reader must read the whole passage to grasp and compare them.
Text can contain numbers and needs no graph paper → 'The reader must read the whole text to understand the data'.
Answer: The reader must read the whole text to understand the data
quiz.mistake: Misunderstands what textual presentation looks like

quiz.q: 'Of the 50 workers in a factory, 35 joined the strike.' This is an example of:
quiz.explain: The data are described in a sentence.
steps: The data (50 workers, 35 on strike) are given in an ordinary sentence.
Rule: data described in words and sentences = textual presentation.
There are no rows, columns or diagrams.
So it is textual presentation.
Answer: Textual presentation
quiz.mistake: Thinks any data with numbers is tabular

quiz.q: In the statement 'Of the 50 workers in a factory, 35 joined the strike', what percentage of workers did NOT join?
steps: Not joined = 50 − 35 = 15
Answer: 30%
quiz.mistake: Gives the percentage who joined (70%)

quiz.q: Which advantage does textual presentation have over a table?
options: It is easier to compare many figures
It allows emphasis on certain points
It is shorter for large data
It removes the need to read
quiz.explain: A writer can stress key facts through sentences.
steps: Asked: an advantage of text over a table.
In sentences, a writer can stress the most important facts.
Tables are better for comparing many figures and for large data.
So text 'allows emphasis on certain points'.
Answer: It allows emphasis on certain points
quiz.mistake: Credits text with the advantages of tables

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Large data are generally not presented in textual form.
Reason (R): In textual form, comparison of many figures is difficult.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because comparing many figures in sentences is hard, large data go into tables or diagrams.
steps: A: large data are generally not presented in text → true.
R: in text, comparing many figures is difficult → true.
Because comparison is hard in sentences, large data go into tables or diagrams.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the drawback to the choice of form

quiz.q: Which form gives the quickest visual impression of the data?
quiz.explain: Diagrams convey patterns at a glance, though less exactly than tables.
steps: Asked: the form that gives the quickest visual impression.
Text and tables must be read figure by figure.
Diagrams show patterns at a glance, though less exactly than tables.
So the answer is 'Diagrammatic'.
Answer: Diagrammatic
quiz.mistake: Confuses exactness with speed of understanding

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I have numbers on how many seeds each bird ate. How can I show them? Is writing a sentence enough?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Three forms: textual for a few figures, tables for detail, diagrams for a quick look!
teach.nudge: Good! But are sentences good when there are lots of numbers? What other forms are there?

revise.summary: Data can be presented in three forms: textual, tabular and diagrammatic. Textual presentation describes data in sentences; it suits small data but makes comparison hard when data are many.
focus: Name the three forms of presentation
Know when textual presentation suits and its drawback
Recognise a textual presentation in a sentence
Know that diagrams give the quickest visual impression
remember: Three forms: textual (descriptive), tabular and diagrammatic
Textual: suits small data and allows emphasis; reader must read the whole text and comparison is hard
traps: Don't forget textual presentation is one of the three forms
A sentence with numbers is textual, not tabular
Diagrams are quickest to grasp but less exact than tables

topics.title: Tabular presentation and classification in tables

learn.hook: A single table in the Census can show literacy for men and women, in villages and cities, for every state. That's the power of rows and columns.
points: A table arranges data in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical). Each box where a row meets a column is a cell.
Qualitative classification in a table: by attributes, e.g. literacy rate by sex (male/female) and location (rural/urban).
Quantitative classification: by measurable classes, e.g. population by age group 0–14, 15–59, 60+.
Temporal classification: by time, e.g. India's exports for 2019, 2020, 2021.
Spatial classification: by place, e.g. share of India's exports going to different countries.

example.q: A table has 3 rows (Rural, Urban, Total) and 3 columns (Male, Female, Total). How many cells does the body have, and what kind of classification is it?
steps: Cells = rows × columns = 3 × 3 = 9
Rural/urban and male/female are attributes
So it is qualitative classification

learn.reallife: RBI's Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy is mostly tables, organised by year (temporal) and by state (spatial).

games.title: Type of classification in the table
items: Literacy rate of males and females
Population in age groups 0–14, 15–59, 60+
Rice output for 2020, 2021, 2022
Workers by marital status
Farms grouped by size: 0–1 ha, 1–2 ha, 2–4 ha
Monthly sales from April to March

games.title: Match the table to its classification

quiz.q: In a table, each box formed where a row and a column meet is called a:
quiz.explain: That box is a cell.
steps: Asked: the name of the box where a row and a column meet.
Rule: that box, holding one figure, is a cell.
Stubs are row headings, captions are column headings, the title names the table.
So the answer is 'Cell'.
Answer: Cell
quiz.mistake: Confuses cells with row or column headings

quiz.q: A table showing literacy rates for males and females in rural and urban areas uses:
quiz.explain: Sex and location type are attributes, so this is qualitative.
steps: The table classifies by sex (male/female) and by area (rural/urban).
Both are attributes, not measured numbers.
Rule: classification by attributes is qualitative.
So it uses qualitative classification.
Answer: Qualitative classification
quiz.mistake: Thinks any table with percentages is quantitative

quiz.q: A table showing the share of India's exports to different countries uses:
quiz.explain: Classifying by country is spatial.
steps: The table classifies exports by country.
Countries are places.
Rule: classification by place is spatial.
So it uses spatial classification.
Answer: Spatial classification
quiz.mistake: Confuses spatial with qualitative

quiz.q: A table showing population by age groups 0–14, 15–59 and 60 and above uses:
quiz.explain: Age is measurable and grouped into classes.
steps: The table groups people by age classes 0–14, 15–59, 60+.
Age is a measurable variable.
Rule: grouping by a measured variable is quantitative classification.
So it uses quantitative classification.
Answer: Quantitative classification
quiz.mistake: Thinks age groups are attributes

quiz.q: A table has 5 rows and 4 columns of data in its body. How many cells does the body have?
quiz.explain: 5 × 4 = 20 cells.
steps: Cells = rows × columns
Answer: 20
quiz.mistake: Adds rows and columns

quiz.q: Rows of a table are arranged:
quiz.explain: Rows run horizontally; columns run vertically.
steps: Asked: the direction in which rows run.
Rows run horizontally (left to right).
Columns run vertically (top to bottom).
So rows are arranged horizontally.
Answer: Horizontally
quiz.mistake: Swaps rows and columns

quiz.q: A table gives sugar production for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022. The classification is:
quiz.explain: Classification by years is temporal (chronological).
steps: The table lists sugar output for 2018 to 2022.
The basis of classification is time (years).
Rule: classification by time is temporal (chronological).
So the answer is 'Temporal'.
Answer: Temporal
quiz.mistake: Thinks a list of years is quantitative classes

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Tables make comparison of data easier than text.
Reason (R): In a table, related figures are placed side by side in rows and columns.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Placing figures side by side is exactly what makes comparison easy.
steps: A: tables make comparison easier than text → true.
R: in a table related figures are placed side by side in rows and columns → true.
Placing figures side by side is exactly what makes comparison easy.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Sees no link between layout and comparability

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly is a table? And can I classify bird data in a table in different ways?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Rows and columns meet in cells, and tables can classify by attribute, class, time or place!
teach.nudge: Good! What do we call the boxes where rows and columns meet? And name some ways to classify data in tables.

revise.summary: A table arranges data in rows and columns, and each box where they meet is a cell. Tables classify data qualitatively, quantitatively, temporally or spatially and make comparison easy.
focus: Identify the type of classification used in a table
Count cells in a table body (rows × columns)
Know that rows run horizontally and columns vertically
remember: Cell: the box where a row meets a column
traps: Don't add rows and columns to count cells: multiply them
Don't swap rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical)
A table with percentages is not automatically quantitative; sex and location are attributes

topics.title: Parts of a table and rules of a good table

learn.hook: A table without a title or unit is like a cricket scorecard without team names. You see numbers but can't tell what they mean.
points: One-way table: data classified by one characteristic; two-way: by two characteristics; three-way: by three characteristics.
Table number (for reference) and title (what, where, when, in brief, placed at the top).
Captions are the column headings; stubs are the row headings. The body holds the actual data.
Unit of measurement (e.g. ₹ crore, '000 tonnes) is stated, usually with the title or headings. Source says where the data came from; a note explains anything special, placed below the table.
Large figures are rounded and the unit stated (e.g. 12,34,56,789 written as 12.35 crore).

example.q: Convert into a table: 'In 2011, literacy was 82% among males and 65% among females; in 2001 it was 75% among males and 54% among females.'
steps: Title: Literacy rate in India by sex, 2001 and 2011 (in %)
Stubs (rows): 2001, 2011
Captions (columns): Male, Female
example.answer: A two-way table with years as stubs and sex as captions.

learn.reallife: Every table in the Economic Survey carries a title, unit, and a source line such as 'Source: NSO, MoSPI'.

games.title: Match the part of the table
pairs: Brief statement of contents at the top

games.title: Reading a table from top to bottom
games.prompt: Arrange the parts from top to bottom of a typical table
items: Table number
Title
Captions (column headings)
Body with stubs
Source and note

quiz.q: Column headings of a table are called:
quiz.explain: Captions head the columns.
steps: Asked: the name for column headings.
Rule: column headings = captions; row headings = stubs.
The body holds the figures; notes explain points.
So the answer is 'Captions'.
Answer: Captions
quiz.mistake: Swaps captions and stubs

quiz.q: Row headings of a table are called:
quiz.explain: Stubs head the rows.
steps: Asked: the name for row headings.
Rule: row headings = stubs; column headings = captions.
Titles name the whole table; sources give the origin of data.
So the answer is 'Stubs'.
Answer: Stubs
quiz.mistake: Swaps stubs and captions

quiz.q: The part of a table that tells the reader where the data were obtained from is the:
quiz.explain: The source line names the origin of the data.
steps: Asked: the part that tells where the data came from.
Rule: the source line names the origin of the data.
A note explains a figure; the title names the table; a stub heads a row.
So the answer is 'Source'.
Answer: Source
quiz.mistake: Confuses the source with an explanatory note

quiz.q: A table classifies workers by gender and by location (rural/urban). It is a:
quiz.explain: Two characteristics make it a two-way table.
steps: The table uses two characteristics: gender and location.
Rule: number of characteristics = 'way' of the table.
2 characteristics → two-way table.
So it is a two-way table.
Answer: Two-way table
quiz.mistake: Counts categories instead of characteristics

quiz.q: A table classifies students by gender, by stream (Science/Commerce/Arts) and by result (pass/fail). It is a:
quiz.explain: Three characteristics make it a three-way table.
steps: The table uses gender, stream and result.
Rule: number of characteristics = 'way' of the table.
3 characteristics → three-way table.
So it is a three-way table.
Answer: Three-way table
quiz.mistake: Counts only the main headings

quiz.q: ₹4,56,78,90,000 rounded to crore (one crore = 1,00,00,000) and to two decimals is how many crore?
steps: 1 crore = 1,00,00,000 (10 million)
≈ 456.79 crore
Answer: 456.79
quiz.mistake: Miscounts the zeros in a crore

quiz.q: Where is the title of a table normally placed?
quiz.explain: The title sits at the top, after the table number.
steps: Asked: where a table's title is placed.
Rule: the title comes at the top, just after the table number.
The source and notes go at the bottom.
So the title is placed at the top.
Answer: At the top
quiz.mistake: Confuses the title with the footnote

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A good table must state the unit of measurement.
Reason (R): Without the unit, the figures in the body cannot be correctly understood.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: '45' could mean ₹45 or 45 crore tonnes; the unit gives meaning.
steps: A: a good table must state the unit of measurement → true.
R: without the unit the figures cannot be correctly understood → true.
'45' could mean ₹45 or 45 crore tonnes; the unit gives the figure its meaning.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the unit is optional decoration

quiz.q: You convert this passage into a table: 'In 2011, literacy was 82% among males and 65% among females; in 2001 it was 75% among males and 54% among females.' If the years 2001 and 2011 are the stubs, what are the captions?
quiz.explain: Stubs are the row headings (here the years), so the column headings (captions) are the other characteristic: Male and Female. The figures 75, 54, 82, 65 go in the body.
steps: Stubs (rows) = 2001, 2011
The other characteristic, sex, becomes the captions (columns): Male, Female
Answer: Male and Female
quiz.mistake: Mixes up stubs and captions, or treats body figures as headings

teach.ask: Gappu made a table of seed counts but wrote no title or headings. 'Why can't anyone understand it? Teach me the parts of a table!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Number, title, captions, stubs, body, unit, source and note. My table makes sense now!
teach.nudge: Good! But what are the column and row headings called? And how will readers know the unit and source?

revise.summary: A good table has a table number, title, captions (column headings), stubs (row headings), body, unit of measurement, source and note. Tables are one-way, two-way or three-way by the number of characteristics.
focus: Name the parts of a table and where each goes
Classify a table as one-way, two-way or three-way
Convert a passage into a table
Round large figures and state the unit
remember: Captions: column headings; stubs: row headings; body: the actual data
Title (what, where, when) at the top; source and note below the table
traps: Don't swap captions and stubs
Count characteristics, not categories, to decide one-way, two-way or three-way
Don't treat the unit as optional: without it figures have no clear meaning

topics.title: Bar diagrams: simple, multiple and component

learn.hook: In one glance at a bar chart, you can see which state grows the most rice. That speed is why diagrams exist, even though tables are more exact.
points: Diagrams give a quick, attractive picture of data and help memory, but they are less exact than tables.
Simple bar diagram: bars of equal width with equal gaps; only the height (length) shows the value. Used for discrete variables, attributes, time series and non-frequency data.
Multiple bar diagram: two or more bars drawn side by side for each category to compare data sets, e.g. literacy in 2001 and 2011 for each state.
Component (sub-divided) bar diagram: each bar is split into parts showing components of a total, e.g. enrolment split into boys and girls.
Percentage component bar: every bar has height 100 and the parts show percentage shares.

example.q: A school has 300 students: 120 in Science, 105 in Commerce, 75 in Arts. In a percentage component bar, what heights do the three parts have?

learn.reallife: News channels on results day use multiple bar diagrams to compare seats won by parties in two elections, side by side.

games.title: Match the data to the diagram
pairs: Rice output of 5 states in one year
Literacy of males and females in 4 states
Total cost split into raw material, labour and overheads
Percentage shares of crops in each state, bars all equal to 100

games.title: Bar facts
items: In a simple bar diagram, the width of bars shows the value.
Only the height shows the value; widths are equal and arbitrary.
Bars in a bar diagram have equal gaps between them.
Equal spacing is a rule of bar diagrams.
In a percentage component bar, each bar's total height is 100.
Parts show percentage shares of the total.
Diagrams are more exact than tables.
Tables give exact values; diagrams are approximate.
Multiple bars place bars for different series side by side.
This allows direct comparison.

quiz.q: In a simple bar diagram, the value of each item is shown by the bar's:
quiz.explain: Only the height carries the value; all widths are equal.
steps: Asked: which feature of a bar shows its value in a simple bar diagram.
All bars have equal width and equal gaps.
Only the height (length) changes with the value.
So the value is shown by the bar's height.
Answer: Height (length)
quiz.mistake: Thinks width also represents value as in a histogram

quiz.q: To compare literacy rates of males and females across five states, the best diagram is a:
quiz.explain: Side-by-side bars for males and females compare two series per state.
steps: Two series (males and females) must be compared for each of five states.
A multiple bar diagram puts the bars for males and females side by side.
A simple bar shows one series; a pie shows parts of one whole; an ogive shows cumulative frequency.
So the best choice is a multiple bar diagram.
Answer: Multiple bar diagram
quiz.mistake: Uses a simple bar that shows only one series

quiz.q: A component bar diagram is used to show:
quiz.explain: Each bar is divided into components of the total.
steps: Asked: what a component bar diagram shows.
Each bar stands for a total and is divided into parts.
So it shows the components (parts) of a total.
It is not for cumulative frequencies or densities → 'Parts of a total'.
Answer: Parts of a total
quiz.mistake: Confuses component bars with ogives

quiz.q: A household spends ₹12,000 out of ₹40,000 on food. In a percentage component bar, the food portion has height:
steps: Answer: 30
quiz.mistake: Writes the rupee figure instead of the percentage

quiz.q: In a percentage component bar for a firm, wages are 45 and raw materials are 35. If the rest is profit, what is the height of the profit portion?
steps: Total = 100
Answer: 20
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the full bar height is 100

quiz.q: Which is NOT a rule of a bar diagram?
options: Bars should touch each other without gaps
Bars start from a common baseline
quiz.explain: Bar diagrams have gaps between bars; touching bars belong to histograms.
steps: Rules of a bar diagram: equal widths, equal spacing, common baseline.
So bars have gaps between them.
Touching bars without gaps are a feature of a histogram.
So 'Bars should touch each other without gaps' is NOT a rule.
Answer: Bars should touch each other without gaps
quiz.mistake: Mixes up bar diagrams and histograms

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Bar diagrams can be used for qualitative data such as religion or occupation.
Reason (R): A bar diagram needs a continuous variable on the x-axis.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Bar diagrams suit attributes and discrete data; it is the histogram that needs a continuous variable.
steps: A: bar diagrams can show qualitative data like religion or occupation → true.
R: a bar diagram needs a continuous variable on the x-axis → false.
It is the histogram that needs a continuous variable.
So A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Applies the histogram's rule to bar diagrams

quiz.q: Rice output (million tonnes): State A 16, State B 12, State C 8. If 1 cm represents 4 million tonnes, the bar for State B is how long?
steps: Length = value / scale
Answer: 3 cm
quiz.mistake: Uses the value itself as the length

items: State A
State B
State C

teach.ask: Gappu wants to show how many berries birds ate in each forest, and split each bar by bird type. 'Which bar diagram do I use?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Simple bars for one series, multiple bars side by side, component bars for parts. Heights show values!
teach.nudge: Good! But which bar shows parts of a total? And what does the height of a bar show?

revise.summary: Bar diagrams give a quick picture of data. Simple bars show one series, multiple bars compare series side by side, and component bars split a total into parts; only the height shows the value.
focus: Choose between simple, multiple and component bar diagrams
Work out heights for a percentage component bar
Know the rules: equal width, equal gaps, height shows value
Convert values to bar lengths using a scale
remember: Simple bar: equal width and equal gaps; only the height (length) shows the value
Percentage component bar: every bar has height 100 and parts show percentage shares
traps: In a bar diagram width does not show value; that is a histogram's rule
Bars should not touch: touching bars belong to histograms
Bar diagrams can show qualitative data; only histograms need a continuous variable

learn.hook: Every rupee the Union Government spends can be shown as one pie: interest, defence, subsidies, states' share... Each slice's angle tells its share.
points: A pie diagram is a circle divided into sectors, each sector showing a component's share of the total.
Sector angle = (component value ÷ total) × 360°. If shares are already in percent, angle = percentage × 3.6°.
All the sector angles add up to 360° and all percentages to 100.

Pie diagrams suit data showing parts of a whole at one point of time (e.g. budget shares, religious or occupational composition). They do not suit time series like monthly rainfall, where a bar diagram or line graph is better.

example.q: A family spends: food ₹8,000, rent ₹6,000, education ₹4,000, others ₹2,000. Find the sector angles.

learn.reallife: The Budget at a Glance document shows 'Rupee comes from' and 'Rupee goes to' as pie charts every year.

games.title: Is a pie diagram suitable?
items: Shares of different crops in total farm area
Monthly rainfall over 12 months

quiz.q: In a pie diagram, the sector angle for a component that is 40% of the total is:
steps: Angle = % × 3.6
Answer: 144°
quiz.mistake: Uses the percentage as the angle directly

quiz.q: A sector of 54° represents what percentage of the total?
steps: % = angle / 3.6
Answer: 15%
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing

quiz.q: Out of ₹5,000 monthly expenses, a student spends ₹1,250 on books. The sector angle for books is:
steps: Answer: 90°
quiz.mistake: Gives the percentage (25) instead of the angle

quiz.q: In a pie diagram, the sum of all sector angles is:
quiz.explain: A full circle measures 360°.
steps: A pie diagram is a full circle.
A full circle measures 360°.
All sector angles together make up the whole circle.
So the sum of all sector angles = 360°.
Answer: 360°
quiz.mistake: Confuses angles with percentages (which add to 100)

quiz.q: A pie diagram has three components. Two of them have angles of 150° and 120°. What is the angle of the third component?
steps: Total = 360°
Answer: 90°
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 180° or adds the two angles

quiz.q: Which data are LEAST suitable for a pie diagram?
options: Shares of sectors in GDP in one year
Monthly rainfall in Mumbai over a year
Share of expenditure items in a family budget
quiz.explain: Monthly rainfall is a time series, not parts of one whole; a bar diagram or line graph suits it.
steps: A pie diagram shows the parts of one whole.
GDP shares, family budget items and students by stream are all parts of one total.
Monthly rainfall is a time series, not parts of a whole; a bar diagram or line graph suits it.
So monthly rainfall is least suitable.
Answer: Monthly rainfall in Mumbai over a year
quiz.mistake: Thinks any set of numbers can be shown as a pie

quiz.q: A town's population is 60% Hindi speakers, 25% Marathi speakers and the rest others. What is the sector angle for 'others'?
steps: Others = 15%
Answer: 54°
quiz.mistake: Uses 15 as the angle without multiplying by 3.6

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A pie diagram is suitable for showing components of a whole.
Reason (R): The angles of all sectors together make up the full circle of 360°, representing the total.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the circle stands for the total, its slices naturally show parts of the whole.
steps: A: a pie diagram suits components of a whole → true.
R: all sector angles together make 360°, representing the total → true.
Because the circle stands for the total, its slices naturally show the parts.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the full circle to the whole

teach.ask: Gappu ate 4 berries, 3 worms and 5 seeds today. 'Can I show my meal as a pie? How do I get the angles?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Each share of the total times 360° gives a slice: berries 120°, worms 90°, seeds 150°!
teach.nudge: Good! But how do I turn a share into an angle? What does the whole circle measure?

revise.summary: A pie diagram is a circle divided into sectors, each showing a component's share of the total. Sector angle = (component ÷ total) × 360°, and all angles add up to 360°.
focus: Calculate sector angles from values or percentages
Convert an angle back to a percentage
Find a missing sector angle
Know which data suit a pie diagram and which do not
remember: Sector angle = (component value ÷ total) × 360°; from percent, angle = percentage × 3.6°
All sector angles add up to 360° and all percentages to 100
traps: Don't use the percentage as the angle: multiply by 3.6
To go from angle to percentage, divide by 3.6, don't multiply
A time series like monthly rainfall does not suit a pie diagram

learn.hook: A histogram looks like a bar diagram with its bars squeezed together. But the missing gaps carry real meaning.
points: A histogram is a set of adjacent rectangles drawn on class intervals of a continuous variable; the area of each rectangle is proportional to the class frequency.
It is used only for continuous data (classes in exclusive form, so inclusive classes must first be adjusted). There are no gaps between rectangles.
With equal classes, heights can be the frequencies. With unequal classes, heights are frequency densities = frequency ÷ class width.

Mode can be located from a histogram: join the top-right corner of the tallest rectangle to the top-right corner of the rectangle before it, and its top-left corner to the top-left corner of the rectangle after it; the x-value directly below the point where these two lines cross is the mode.
Histogram vs bar diagram: in a histogram both width and height matter (area shows frequency); in a bar diagram only height matters, bars have equal width and gaps.

example.q: Classes 0–10 (f = 5), 10–30 (f = 20), 30–35 (f = 10). Find the heights for a histogram.
steps: Widths are unequal: 10, 20, 5.
Density = f / width.

learn.reallife: Hospitals plot histograms of patients' waiting times to see where most patients wait, and to spot the modal waiting time.

games.title: Histogram or bar?
items: A histogram has gaps between rectangles.
Rectangles are adjacent because the variable is continuous.
In a histogram the area of a rectangle is proportional to frequency.
That is the defining rule.
A histogram can be drawn for qualitative data like religion.
It needs a continuous variable.
With unequal classes, heights should be frequency densities.
Density = frequency ÷ width keeps areas proportional.
Mode can be estimated graphically from a histogram.
Using the tallest rectangle and its neighbours.
In a bar diagram, bar width matters.
Only height matters in a bar diagram.

quiz.q: A histogram can be drawn only for:
quiz.explain: Its rectangles stand on continuous class intervals.
steps: Asked: the data for which a histogram can be drawn.
A histogram's rectangles stand on class intervals that run into each other.
That needs continuous data.
Qualitative or gapped discrete data suit bar diagrams → 'Continuous data'.
Answer: Continuous data
quiz.mistake: Thinks histograms suit any data

quiz.q: In a histogram, the frequency of a class is proportional to the rectangle's:
quiz.explain: Area (width × height) represents frequency.
steps: Rule: in a histogram, frequency is shown by the area of the rectangle.
Area = width × height.
With equal widths, height alone also works, but in general it is area.
So frequency is proportional to the rectangle's area.
Answer: Area
quiz.mistake: Applies the bar diagram rule

quiz.q: Class 20–40 has frequency 30. If classes are unequal, the height of its rectangle (frequency density) is:
steps: Density = 30/20 = 1.5
Answer: 1.5
quiz.mistake: Uses the frequency itself as height with unequal classes

quiz.q: Classes 0–5 (f = 10) and 5–15 (f = 10). Which rectangle is taller in the histogram?
quiz.explain: Densities: 10/5 = 2 and 10/10 = 1. Equal frequencies spread over a wider class give a shorter rectangle.
steps: Unequal widths → height = frequency density = frequency ÷ width.
2 > 1, so 0–5 is taller: height 2 versus 1.
Answer: 0–5, height 2 versus 1
quiz.mistake: Uses raw frequency as height despite unequal widths

quiz.q: Inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29 must be converted before drawing a histogram because:
options: Histograms need continuous classes without gaps
quiz.explain: The gaps (19 to 20) must be removed: 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
steps: Classes 10–19, 20–29 leave a gap between 19 and 20.
A histogram needs continuous classes without gaps.
So adjust by 0.5 each side: 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
Hence the conversion is needed because histograms need continuous classes.
Answer: Histograms need continuous classes without gaps
quiz.mistake: Does not see the gap problem

quiz.q: Which can be located graphically using a histogram?
quiz.explain: The mode is found from the tallest rectangle and lines to its neighbours.
steps: Asked: the average that can be found graphically from a histogram.
Draw lines from the top corners of the tallest rectangle to its neighbours' corners.
The x-value where they cross is the mode.
The median uses ogives; the mean is calculated → 'Mode'.
Answer: Mode
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the median, which is found from ogives

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a histogram, rectangles are drawn without gaps.
Reason (R): The class intervals of a continuous variable are continuous, with no breaks between them.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Continuous classes run into each other, so the rectangles touch.
steps: A: rectangles in a histogram are drawn without gaps → true.
R: classes of a continuous variable have no breaks between them → true.
Because the classes run into each other, the rectangles must touch.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks gaps are just a style choice

quiz.q: A class 50–60 has frequency 12 and the next class 60–80 has frequency 12. What is the frequency density of 60–80?
quiz.explain: Width = 20, density = 12/20 = 0.6.
steps: Density = 12/20 = 0.6
Answer: 0.6
quiz.mistake: Divides by 10 out of habit instead of by the actual width

teach.ask: Gappu drew bars with gaps for bird weights 10–20 g, 20–30 g. 'Is that a histogram? What makes a histogram special?'
teach.praise: Tweet! No gaps for continuous classes, area shows frequency, use density for unequal classes, and it even shows the mode!
teach.nudge: Nice try! Should the rectangles have gaps for continuous data? And what shows the frequency: height or area?

revise.summary: A histogram is a set of adjacent rectangles on class intervals of a continuous variable, with area proportional to class frequency. With unequal classes, heights are frequency densities; the mode can be located from it.

Contrast a histogram with a bar diagram
remember: In a histogram area shows frequency; in a bar diagram only height matters

Divide by the actual class width, not 10 out of habit
The median is found from ogives, not from a histogram

topics.title: Frequency polygon, frequency curve and ogives

learn.hook: Draw two ogives on the same graph and something magical happens: the point where they cross drops straight down to the median.
points: Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of the tops of histogram rectangles with straight lines, and close it by joining to the mid-points of zero-frequency classes at both ends. Or plot frequency against class marks directly.
Frequency curve: a smooth freehand curve drawn through the points of the frequency polygon.
Less-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('less than' the upper limit) plotted against upper class limits; it rises from left to right.
More-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('more than' the lower limit) plotted against lower class limits; it falls from left to right.
The two ogives intersect at a point whose x-coordinate is the median.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have frequencies 4, 6, 8, 2. Find the less-than and more-than cumulative frequencies.

learn.reallife: Board result analysts use ogives to read off how many students scored below 33% or above 90% without listing every score.

games.title: Match the graph to its rule
pairs: Cumulative frequency vs upper limits, rising
Cumulative frequency vs lower limits, falling
Mid-points of rectangle tops joined by lines
Smooth freehand curve through polygon points

games.title: Drawing a less-than ogive
items: Find the cumulative frequencies by adding upward
Pair each with its upper class limit
Plot the points on a graph
Join the points with a smooth curve

quiz.q: A less-than ogive is drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against:
quiz.explain: 'Less than' totals are measured up to the upper limit of each class.
steps: 'Less than' means all values below a certain point.
The cumulative total up to a class is complete only at its upper limit.
So the less-than ogive plots cumulative frequency against upper class limits.
Lower limits are used for the more-than ogive.
Answer: Upper class limits
quiz.mistake: Swaps the rules for the two ogives

quiz.q: A more-than ogive generally:
quiz.explain: 'More than' totals get smaller as the lower limit increases.
steps: A more-than ogive plots 'more than lower limit' totals.
As the lower limit increases, fewer values are above it.
So the cumulative frequencies get smaller.
The curve falls from left to right.
Answer: Falls from left to right
quiz.mistake: Thinks all cumulative curves rise

quiz.q: The median of a distribution can be found graphically from:
options: The intersection of less-than and more-than ogives
quiz.explain: The x-value of the meeting point of the two ogives is the median.
steps: Asked: how to find the median graphically.
Draw the less-than and the more-than ogive on the same axes.
Their meeting point has y = N/2.
The x-value of that intersection is the median.
Answer: The intersection of less-than and more-than ogives
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the mode, which is found from a histogram

quiz.q: Frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5 for classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40. What is the 'less than 30' cumulative frequency?
steps: Answer: 25
quiz.mistake: Takes only the frequency of the 20–30 class

quiz.q: Same data (5, 8, 12, 5 for 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40). What is the 'more than 20' cumulative frequency?
steps: Answer: 17
quiz.mistake: Includes the 10–20 class or only one class

quiz.q: A frequency polygon is closed at both ends by:
options: Joining to the mid-points of imaginary zero-frequency classes
Joining the first and last points directly
quiz.explain: Extending to zero-frequency classes on each side closes the polygon on the x-axis.
steps: Asked: how a frequency polygon is closed at both ends.
Add an imaginary class with zero frequency before the first and after the last class.
Join the end points to the mid-points of these classes on the x-axis.
So it is closed by joining to the mid-points of zero-frequency classes.
Answer: Joining to the mid-points of imaginary zero-frequency classes
quiz.mistake: Does not know how the polygon is closed

quiz.q: Less-than and more-than ogives meet at a point where x = 34 and y = 25. What is the median?
quiz.explain: The median is the x-coordinate of the intersection: 34. (The y-value 25 is N/2.)
steps: Rule: the median is the x-coordinate where the two ogives meet.
Given meeting point: x = 34, y = 25.
y = 25 is N/2, not the median.
So the median = 34.
Answer: 34
quiz.mistake: Reads the y-coordinate instead of the x-coordinate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A frequency curve is drawn as a smooth freehand curve.
Reason (R): It is drawn through the points of a frequency polygon to smooth out its sharp corners.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Smoothing the polygon's points gives the frequency curve.
steps: A: a frequency curve is drawn as a smooth freehand curve → true.
R: it is drawn through the frequency polygon's points to smooth its sharp corners → true.
Smoothing the polygon's corners is what produces the curve.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the curve is drawn with straight lines

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are ogives? How can two curves tell me the median wing span of my flock?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Less-than ogive uses upper limits, more-than uses lower limits, and where they cross is the median!
teach.nudge: Good! Which limits are used for each ogive? And what happens where they meet?

revise.summary: A frequency polygon joins the mid-points of histogram tops and a frequency curve smooths it. A less-than ogive plots cumulative frequencies against upper limits, a more-than ogive against lower limits; they meet at the median.
focus: Find less-than and more-than cumulative frequencies
Know what each ogive is plotted against and its direction
Read the median from the intersection of the ogives
Know how a frequency polygon is closed
remember: Less-than ogive: against upper class limits, rises; more-than ogive: against lower class limits, falls
The x-coordinate of the ogives' intersection is the median
traps: Don't swap the rules of the two ogives
Read the x-coordinate of the intersection for the median, not the y-coordinate
A frequency curve is drawn freehand and smooth, not with straight lines

topics.title: Arithmetic line graphs and choosing a diagram

learn.hook: Plot India's exports and imports year by year on one graph and the widening gap between the two lines tells the trade deficit story without a single sentence.
points: An arithmetic line graph (time series graph) plots time on the x-axis and the value of the variable on the y-axis; points are joined by straight lines.
It shows trends, cycles and seasonal ups and downs, e.g. monthly vegetable prices or yearly GDP growth.
Multiple line graphs plot two or more series on the same axes for comparison, e.g. exports and imports, or growth rates of agriculture, industry and services.

Choosing a diagram: time series → line graph or bar diagram; parts of a whole → pie or component bar; continuous frequency distribution → histogram, polygon or ogive; categories → simple or multiple bar.

example.q: Which diagram suits each? (a) monthly rainfall in Chennai, (b) share of food, rent and travel in a budget, (c) heights of 200 students in classes, (d) sectoral growth rates over 10 years.
steps: (a) A time series: bar diagram or line graph.
(b) Parts of a whole: pie diagram.
(c) Continuous frequency distribution: histogram.
(d) Several time series: multiple line graph.
example.answer: (a) bar/line graph, (b) pie, (c) histogram, (d) multiple line graph

learn.reallife: RBI and MoSPI release charts of monthly CPI inflation as line graphs, making it easy to see if inflation is rising or easing.

The horizontal axis shows years, months etc.
A line graph is suitable for showing trends over time.
Rising or falling lines show the trend.
Two series cannot be shown on one line graph.
A multiple line graph shows two or more series.
A pie diagram is the best way to show a 20-year trend.
A pie shows parts of a whole, not trends.
Seasonal patterns can be seen in a monthly line graph.
Regular ups and downs within a year show seasonality.

quiz.q: In an arithmetic line graph, the x-axis usually shows:
quiz.explain: It is a time series graph, so time goes on the horizontal axis.
steps: An arithmetic line graph is a time series graph.
Time (years, months) goes on the horizontal x-axis.
The value of the variable goes on the y-axis.
So the x-axis usually shows time.
Answer: Time
quiz.mistake: Swaps the axes

quiz.q: Which diagram best compares the growth rates of agriculture, industry and services over 10 years?
quiz.explain: Three time series on the same axes are best compared with a multiple line graph.
steps: Three series (agriculture, industry, services) are to be compared over 10 years.
A multiple line graph plots several time series on the same axes.
A pie shows one whole; a histogram and ogive show frequency distributions.
So the best is a multiple line graph.
Answer: Multiple line graph
quiz.mistake: Picks a pie because there are three sectors

quiz.q: Exports were ₹400 crore and imports ₹550 crore in a year. If both are plotted on a multiple line graph, what is the vertical gap (trade deficit) that year, in ₹ crore?
quiz.explain: Deficit = imports − exports = 550 − 400 = ₹150 crore.
steps: Given: exports = ₹400 crore, imports = ₹550 crore.
Trade deficit = imports − exports.
Vertical gap (trade deficit) = ₹150 crore.
Answer: 150
quiz.mistake: Adds the two series instead of finding the gap

quiz.q: A line graph mainly helps to show:
quiz.explain: It reveals upward or downward movement over time.
steps: A line graph joins values plotted over time.
So it shows whether the values move up or down over time.
Parts of a whole suit a pie; class frequencies suit a histogram; exact values suit a table.
So it mainly shows trends over time.
Answer: Trends over time
quiz.mistake: Confuses with a pie diagram

quiz.q: Which data are best shown by a histogram?
options: Number of students in each stream
Weights of 100 babies in classes 2–2.5 kg, 2.5–3 kg, etc.
quiz.explain: A continuous frequency distribution suits a histogram.
steps: A histogram needs a continuous frequency distribution.
Weights in classes 2–2.5 kg, 2.5–3 kg… are continuous classes.
Students by stream is qualitative; yearly exports is a time series; budget shares suit a pie.
So the baby weights are best shown by a histogram.
Answer: Weights of 100 babies in classes 2–2.5 kg, 2.5–3 kg, etc.
quiz.mistake: Uses a histogram for categories

quiz.q: Vegetable prices rise every summer and fall every winter, year after year. On a monthly line graph, this pattern is called:
quiz.explain: Regular movements within a year are seasonal.
steps: Prices rise every summer and fall every winter, year after year.
Rule: regular ups and downs within each year are seasonal variation.
Correlation and sampling error are different ideas.
So the pattern is seasonal variation.
Answer: Seasonal variation
quiz.mistake: Confuses a seasonal pattern with a long-term trend

quiz.q: A firm's sales were 100, 120, 150 and 180 units in four years. By how many units did sales rise from the first to the last year, as shown by the line graph?
steps: Rise = last − first
Answer: 80
quiz.mistake: Reads only the last value

Common axes make the comparison direct, which is why the graph is useful.
